title: What Do Pastors Do With All Their Time?
author: David de Bruyn
summary: Pastor David de Bruyn answers the common assumption that a pastor works only on Sundays by showing how quickly the real demands of ministry add up to an impossible work week. His central move is to reframe the pastor’s role from doing all the ministry to equipping members to do it, drawing on Ephesians 4. Because demand always exceeds one person’s capacity, the pastor must treat time as a scarce resource and deploy it where it multiplies: first preaching, then raising up faithful leaders, then overseeing and delegating the church’s wider work. He offers a rough weekly budget of hours to show that a diligent pastor easily exceeds forty hours, while conceding with Tozer that a pastor can also become a privileged idler. The piece closes with three takeaways about freeing a pastor financially, expecting equipping rather than all ministry from him, and the virtuous cycle created when members minister to one another.
points: A new members’ class that assigned reasonable hours to each ministry task arrived at roughly a 90-hour week before family, health or rest were counted.
De Bruyn’s answer is delegation: the pastor trains others to counsel, evangelise, organise and teach rather than carrying all the work himself.
Preaching comes first because one hour before 200 people yields 200 hours of ministry, followed by discipling eager leaders and supervising delegated work.
A church that expects one man to deliver personal ministry to every member is, he warns, choosing mediocre ministry, a burnt-out pastor and a disgruntled membership.
quotes: I then asked if the pastor should make time for his family, for fitness and health, for maintenance of his own home and possessions, and possibly for recreation or leisure. They heartily agreed, but couldn’t see where it would fit into this 90-hour work week.

The pastor is to equip members to do the work of the ministry. Much of those 80 hours is supposed to be carried out by the members of the Body, not all by the pastor himself. He trains others to counsel, evangelise, organise, administrate, teach, and indeed, train others.

But since the demands of even a small church far exceed what one man can do, he must treat his time like a precious, scarce resource that must be stewarded efficiently. Consequently, he deploys his time in ways that will result in the most equipping work for the most people.
That means his priority is preaching. If he preaches to 200 people for one hour a week, that’s 200 hours of ministry in one go.
Instead of devoting his time to the lukewarm, undecided and half-committed, he will prioritise the faithful, growing and eager ones, teaching them and counselling them into even greater maturity.

A church should expect equipping from their pastor, but ministry from every member. The pastor is included in that membership, so he will certainly do some of that ministry. But a church which expects sufficient personal ministry to every member from one man is dooming itself to mediocre ministry, a burnt-out pastor, and a disgruntled membership.
